condition_specific: Cancer caused by exposure to a known carcinogen reasonably linked to the disabling cancer
notes: Alabama's benefit for this condition operates outside workers' compensation. Sections 11-43-144 (municipal firefighters) and 36-30-40 (state firefighters) create an employer-paid disability and death benefit, not a workers' compensation presumption -- firefighters must pursue this benefit track rather than filing a standard workers' comp claim. The cancer must develop during service, and the firefighter must show exposure to a carcinogen recognized by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC); the presumption is rebuttable by a preponderance of the evidence. A firefighter who dies of cancer within 10 years of leaving employment is treated as having died in the line of duty (§ 11-43-144(c)(2)); that 10-year window applies only to the death benefit, not to disability claims. This core cancer coverage traces back to the original 1967 municipal law (§ 11-43-144) -- not the October 1, 2026 date, which applies only to the newly added Parkinson's disease coverage. The parallel state-employee provision (§ 36-30-40/41) likely dates to around 2010-2013, based on a grandfather-clause deadline requiring a physical exam by January 1, 2013 for those without one, though its exact original enactment year has not been independently confirmed.

Alabama's benefit for this condition operates outside workers' compensation. Sections 11-43-144 (municipal firefighters) and 36-30-40/36-30-41 (state firefighters) create an employer-paid disability and death benefit, not a workers' compensation presumption -- firefighters must pursue this benefit track rather than filing a standard workers' comp claim. The presumption is rebuttable by a preponderance of the evidence. Both the municipal and state sections cover the same list of occupational diseases (hypertension, cardiovascular and respiratory disease, cancer, HIV, and hepatitis). A pre-employment physical exam is required unless the firefighter was hired before September 8, 1967 (municipal track) or before January 1, 2013 (state track). This coverage traces back to the original 1967 municipal law -- not the October 1, 2026 date, which applies only to the newly added Parkinson's disease coverage. The state-track provision's exact original enactment year has not been independently confirmed, but the 2013 exam deadline suggests it originated around 2010-2013.

condition_specific: Parkinson's disease caused by exposure to a known toxin associated with increased risk
notes: NOTE: Alabama's system operates separately from workers' compensation. §§ 11-43-144 and 36-30-40 create employer disability and death benefits, not a WC presumption. First responders with occupational disease must pursue these employer-benefit tracks, not a standard WC claim. Must manifest during service AND firefighter must demonstrate exposure to known toxin associated with Parkinson's risk. Rebuttable by preponderance. Effective October 1, 2026.
